title: Knowledge Check 9: Lessons 65-68
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 65-68 of the salesforce-architect series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A field-services company wants a technician assistant that answers from its product manuals and can also open follow-up service cases. It currently routes all model traffic through the API gateway that already fronts its REST services. Which gap in that choice does the lesson identify?
options: The gateway rate-limits by request and caches by exact match, so a user can exhaust the budget in long documents and repeated questions reaccrue cost with no multi-provider failover.
The gateway handles token-based rate limiting but not semantic caching, so it should be replaced to save money.
The gateway is fine for model traffic as long as it uses a single provider, because LLM calls behave like any other API call.
The gateway should be removed entirely so each application can pick its own model and provider directly.
questions.explanation: The lesson's first pitfall is that a plain API gateway measures the wrong thing: it rate-limits by request when LLM cost and capacity scale with tokens, caches by exact match so repeated questions reaccrue cost, and fronts a single provider with no failover, which is why the fix is an LLM gateway that understands tokens.

questions.question: In the enterprise AI reference architecture, where does each of the three patterns sit in the stack?
options: RAG spans the data layer and AI/ML layer via a vector store plus retrieval and generation; the agent platform is the agentic layer runtime; the LLM gateway is the model entry point in the AI/ML layer.
RAG sits entirely in the data layer, the agent platform in the infrastructure layer, and the LLM gateway in the experience layer.
All three are components of the integration layer and interchangeable with the API gateway.
The agent platform does RAG and the LLM gateway, so the three are the same component with different names.
questions.explanation: The lesson places RAG where the data layer meets the AI/ML layer (a vector database stores embeddings while retrieval and generation live in the AI/ML layer), the agent platform in the agentic layer as the runtime for reasoning, memory, and tools, and the LLM gateway as the single model entry point in the AI/ML layer.

questions.question: A client plans to deploy a single large hosted model for every agent task, integrated directly into each application. What does the lesson say this decision loses, and what does the LLM gateway restore?
options: It loses a single place to enforce budget, log access, and swap models, and the gateway restores a governed, centralized point where routing, token-based rate limiting, failover, and cost tracking apply and a better model can replace the current one without rewriting consumers.
It loses nothing, because using one model for everything is simpler and cheaper than managing multiple providers.
It loses only the ability to run on-premises, and the gateway restores local model hosting.
It loses the ability to do RAG, and the gateway restores retrieval and generation in one component.
questions.explanation: The lesson's pitfall is that direct provider integration leaves no one place to enforce budget, log access, or swap models, so switching providers means rewriting every caller. The gateway turns model selection into a governed, centralized decision: it routes requests, rate-limits by token, falls back across providers, tracks cost, and lets an architect swap in a better model at the gateway instead of rewriting consumers.

questions.question: A developer merges a change that breaks the integration build. Where does the team find out, and why does that matter?
options: In continuous integration, on the day of the merge, because CI validates every merge to the shared main line and catching the break there is cheap.
At release time, because integration is a separate phase that only runs before production.
In production, because that is the first environment where the change is actually exercised.
Never, because a broken integration build has no effect on the rest of the lifecycle.
questions.explanation: Continuous integration validates every merge to the shared main line, so a change that breaks the build is caught the day it is merged, not the week before release. Catching it in CI is cheap; catching it at release time is not.

questions.question: An audit team asks what changed between the last two releases and who approved it. What does the lesson say you point them at?
options: The change sets stored in the source org, which record every deployment.
The Git history, because source control keeps a full, attributable history of every change.
The production org's setup audit trail, which is the only record of what is live.
A spreadsheet the release manager maintains, since no tool tracks this automatically.
questions.explanation: Source control keeps a full history of changes so a bad change can be rolled back, and it gives quality control, transparency, collaboration, and resilience to risk. The branching and versioning discipline is what makes the 'what changed and who approved it' question answerable from the tool.

questions.question: A release deploys successfully but a flow the release touched starts failing in production. What is missing from the lifecycle?
options: Continuous integration, because the merge was never validated.
A staging environment, because the change was never rehearsed.
Observability, because the team deployed but did not watch the running release.
Source control, because the change cannot be rolled back.
questions.explanation: A deployment that succeeds is not the same as a release that works. Observability is the discipline of understanding a running system from its outputs, and monitoring and feedback on a release are what close the DevOps loop. A deployment that lands and is never watched can fail for a week before anyone notices.

questions.question: A company with 4,000 employees is moving to Salesforce and wants each employee's Salesforce user record to exist before day one and stay continuously in sync with the corporate directory, including automatic deactivation when someone leaves. Which provisioning approach fits this population, and why?
options: Just-in-time provisioning, because it creates the record on first login and requires no integration to build.
SCIM provisioning, because it creates and updates user records through REST operations and keeps the Salesforce user list a faithful mirror of the identity provider.
Manual user creation in Salesforce, because it gives the administrator full control over each record.
Federation only, because it authenticates users without ever creating a Salesforce user record.
questions.explanation: SCIM is the right tool when the user record must exist ahead of time and stay continuously in sync. It creates, updates, and deactivates user objects through REST operations, so the Salesforce user list mirrors the identity provider and deactivates when a person leaves.

questions.question: A user authenticates successfully at the corporate identity provider, but the Salesforce login fails and no matching user is found. Per the lesson, what is the most likely cause?
options: The Federation ID is not set consistently, so the SAML assertion cannot be matched to a Salesforce user.
SCIM provisioning is disabled, so no user records can ever be created.
The user's password is wrong at the identity provider.
Salesforce is acting as the identity provider instead of the service provider.
questions.explanation: The Federation ID is the field on the Salesforce User object that links the Salesforce user to the identity provider's identifier. If it is not set consistently, the SAML assertion cannot match a user, so the user authenticates at the identity provider but the Salesforce login fails.

questions.question: A consultant from a partner firm leaves their company. The company running the Salesforce portal does nothing. How does the consultant lose access to the portal?
options: SCIM deactivates the consultant's record automatically when the partner firm removes them from the directory.
The consultant's Salesforce record expires after a fixed number of days.
The partner's identity provider stops issuing assertions, so the consultant can no longer authenticate to the portal.
The portal administrator receives an alert and manually deactivates the consultant.
questions.explanation: Federation lets each partner's identity provider authenticate their own people. When a partner employee leaves, the partner's identity provider stops issuing assertions, so the person loses access to the portal without the company doing anything.

questions.question: A business wants "fast recovery" for its CRM but has given no other numbers. Per the lesson, what should the architect ask for, and how should the targets be scoped?
options: A single org-wide uptime percentage that everyone should meet with one uniform target
A measurable RTO and RPO per business capability, approved by business stakeholders, because critical and non-critical data do not warrant the same target
The name of the backup product the company prefers, since tooling alone decides recovery speed
A confirmation from the vendor that platform-level redundancy is enough, with no customer-side targets needed
questions.explanation: Salesforce's Well-Architected framework sets RTO and RPO per business capability rather than uniformly, and requires business stakeholder approval. A single uniform target is itself flagged as an anti-pattern.

questions.question: An org relies only on monthly Data Export Service exports as its backup. The lesson identifies which achievable recovery reality from this arrangement?
options: Automatic restoration of accidentally deleted records, because an export recovers the Recycle Bin
A worst case data loss of roughly a month, a 48 hour download window after each job, and deleted records excluded because the Recycle Bin is not exported
Real time recovery down to the last transactional second, since exports capture every change as it happens
Guaranteed restore within an hour, because export files are always immediately accessible on the platform
questions.explanation: Monthly exports carry a manual generation window of 29 days, files are only downloadable for 48 hours after completion, and data export excludes the Recycle Bin, so deleted records do not return through an export.

questions.question: A client wants a near-zero RPO on financial records but currently only takes daily backups. What does the lesson say is required beyond a more frequent backup?
options: Nothing; daily backups are sufficient to guarantee a near-zero RPO
A secondary data center added to the same org so it becomes active-active automatically
A replication mechanism such as asynchronous event streaming or Change Data Capture, because daily backups alone cap the RPO at a day
A legally binding service level agreement with the vendor that waives any data loss
questions.explanation: Near-zero RPO for financial transactions requires event-driven asynchronous replication, and minute-level RPO can use Change Data Capture. A daily backup cannot produce a sub-day recovery point.
